title: 4. Industry Structure, Competitive Moat & External Learning Hub

epigraph.quote: A moat is not what a vendor says it owns; it is what the customer would have to rebuild if the vendor walked out tomorrow.
epigraph.author: Outsourced-Services Underwriting Rule

web_blocks.html: MPS does not sit in 'publishing'. It sits in the plumbing between a researcher's manuscript and a reader's screen. Since FY26 it also sits between a clinical fact and a nurse's phone. The scholarly chain runs from author to journal (editor and peer reviewers), then publisher, platform and finally library or institution. MPS sells into four of those links. They are the author (AJE editing and pre-submission review), the editorial office (peer-review administration), the publisher's production line (copyediting, composition, XML, accessibility) and the platform layer (HighWire, DigiCore Pro, Think365) [1, 25, 38]. The payer is almost always the publisher, society or university press, not the reader. That one fact shapes the industry. A handful of very large buyers negotiate with a long tail of vendors.

web_blocks.takeaway: Read down the 'Main pressure' column. Every link faces AI, but in different ways. Production faces price deflation. The editorial office faces volume and in-sourcing. Platforms face lower switching cost. Clinical content faces chatbots. A single 'AI risk' label hides four different business problems. MPS's exposure is not equal across them.

web_blocks.html: Now the size of the pond. The STM trade association's 2021 Global Brief, quoting Outsell, put the global STM publishing market at $27 billion in 2018, $28 billion in 2019 and $26.5 billion in 2020 (a pandemic dip). Article output grew 5 to 6.5% a year over 2015 to 2020, while the count of journals grew only 2 to 3% [49]. Delta Think's 2026 update sizes the narrower scholarly journals market at just under $10 billion in 2025. That is up about 8%, helped by an open access recovery, AI licensing deals and currency. Delta Think expects growth to fall back to 5.7% a year over 2025 to 2028 [50]. Open access (OA) is the engine. The OA market was about $3.4 billion in 2025, up just over 20%. Some 52% of articles were published OA, but only about a third of market value [50]. In plain English, the system earns less per OA article but moves far more articles. An outsourced vendor's volume follows article count, not journal revenue.

web_blocks.takeaway: The honest picture is a slow-growing, concentrated value pool with fast-growing unit volumes underneath. A vendor wins when volume growth exceeds the unit-price give-back. That is the equation management described on the Q2 FY27 call. The outsourced content-services slice has no credible published size. I could not find one from a source I could open, so I do not quote one.

web_blocks.html: Consolidation of buyers matters as much as growth. The largest publishers, of which Springer Nature (2025 revenue EUR 1,926.4m) is one, are big, profitable and growing [52]. Management says on the Q2 FY27 call that 'the largest companies in our market are consolidating toward the partners that they trust the most' [2]. The top-15 customers took 58.0% of consolidated revenue in FY26, down from 61.1% in FY25. The single largest customer took 17.3%, down from 18.6%. These are computed from the AR26 concentration note: INR 446.00 Cr of INR 768.37 Cr, and INR 133.17 Cr [1]. Management says the top five fell to 46% of revenue in Q2 FY27 from 51% a year earlier [2]. Vendor consolidation cuts both ways. It raises your share of wallet at the survivors. It also hands the buyer an RFP at which every incumbent must re-bid.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: Count the units, not the dollars
paragraphs: When an industry's dollar market grows mid-single-digit but article counts grow faster, a vendor paid per unit lives in the gap. Suppose a publisher's output grows 5 to 6% a year [49] and unit prices fall 5%. The vendor's revenue is flat. Its cost base has to fall, or it is quietly losing. That arithmetic, not the headline TAM, is what you should keep in mind through the rest of this chapter.

Notice what the CEO told the Q2 FY27 call about pricing: 'With pricing as well, you know, Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume, and that’s where the margin kind of comes from.' [2] That sentence is the whole industry in miniature. The moat audit that follows tests whether it will keep being true.

web_blocks.html: Research integrity is the newest demand driver, and it has a body count. Wiley retracted more than 1,700 Hindawi papers. It began in 2022 with more than 500 tied to peer-review rings. Integrity became a budget line, and Wiley later launched an AI 'Papermill Detection' service with Sage and IEEE [54, 55]. Publishers then pooled their defences in the STM Integrity Hub [56]. Management argues this creates work because it 'sits on top of the production and peer review workflows we already run' [2]. Christine Miranda told the same call that 'The hard problem in research is no longer producing content.' [2] There is a counterweight. Springer Nature acquired Slimmer AI's science division to run its own checks. Integra already markets research-integrity and peer-review services to the same buyers [41, 57]. Integrity is real demand, but it is contested demand.

Education publishing and corporate learning are different animals. In education, work comes in waves. One wave follows US state adoptions: Florida's math adoption now, California next, per the Q2 FY27 call. Another follows accessibility deadlines that force every publisher to remediate content [2, 58]. The catch is that accessibility is also where every vendor now sells AI alt-text. That includes codemantra, S4Carlisle's NINJA platform and MPS's own automation. A fast-growing line may therefore commoditize quickly [58, 59, 25]. Corporate learning is large but cyclical and project-based. Skillsoft's Q3 FY26 revenue was $129 million, down 6%. Its Global Knowledge arm was down 18% and under strategic review [48]. Learning Technologies Group bought GP Strategies in 2021 and went private under General Atlantic on 31 March 2025 [60]. MPS's Corporate Learning is 13% of FY26 revenue (INR 96.0 Cr). Cost action repaired it, not demand. Margins reached 25% in H1 FY27 against about 16%. EBITDA rose 77% with 19% fewer people [1, 2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Two facts stand out. First, MPS's closest scholarly peers are almost all private and disclose no financials. The only listed apples-to-apples reference is Datamatics, and its publishing arm is not broken out. Second, every named competitor sells the same AI pitch. So 'we have AI' differentiates no one. Management said on the Q4 FY25 call that its largest competitor grew from about $115 million of revenue to roughly $400 to 500 million over MPS's journey. The scale gap to the leader is real [20].

web_blocks.html: What distinguishes MPS is not that it does production at lower cost. It is that it owns a layered stack. At the bottom is production: DigiCore, launched at the 2012 Frankfurt Book Fair. Above it sits editorial and peer review, built on AJE capacity. Above that are platforms and hosting (HighWire, DigiCore Pro, Think365). Then, in a different market altogether, come clinical knowledge subscriptions through Unbound [42, 1]. Management says customers 'now buy three and four lines of work from us, when they once bought one' [2]. Its 'star account' programme lifted the average number of MPS business units per star account from 2.5 to 5.5 over two years [18]. That cross-sell index is the best single piece of evidence for embeddedness I have found. It counts integrated relationships instead of adjectives.

web_blocks.takeaway: My scoring averages roughly 3 out of 5. That is a respectable moat, not a wide one. The strongest moats are relationships and Unbound's retention, both 4s. The ones management mentions most loudly (certifications, 'AI-first', labour cost) are 2s and 3s. A durable moat here is relational and workflow-based, not technological. Technology is the part competitors can copy in a year.

web_blocks.html: Now the vulnerabilities, stated as plainly as the strengths. Per-unit price deflation is real. Scholarly Kitchen's November 2025 workflow map says production vendors are automating copyediting, typesetting and proofing with AI. Publishers 'are also evaluating and developing in-house solutions to reduce costs and vendor dependencies' [43]. Concentration is also real. Three customers each exceeded 10% of the standalone company's FY26 revenue. Together they accounted for INR 171.06 Cr, which is 39.0% of standalone revenue (computed from INR 17,105.50 lakh over INR 43,825.57 lakh). FY25 had two such customers [1]. On the consolidated basis one customer alone was INR 133.17 Cr, or 17.3%. In management's words on the Q1 FY26 call, AJE's B2B referral channel was 'entirely dependent on one publisher' [10]. The SaaS-style moat also faces academic challenge. A June 2026 Scholarly Kitchen panel included a Silverchair executive. It expects migration cost to 'come down quite a lot' as agents read and map data between systems [45].

Management says price cuts are recovered in volume; H1 FY27 EBITDA grew 39% on revenue growth of 17.8% [2]
True in direction; so far overcompensated by volume and mix
MPS is mostly hours-based production
Production and accessibility still carry the bulk of revenue; AI alt-text is commoditizing [58]
Management says 25% of revenue is outcome-based and 45% recurring [25]; platforms and Unbound are recurring
Partly true; I cannot verify the exact production share, which is a disclosure gap
Large publishers will in-source
Springer Nature bought Slimmer AI's science division; Scholarly Kitchen cites in-house efforts [41, 43]
Top-5 publisher awarded a large new production mandate and an integrity mandate; top-15 share down to 58.0% [2, 1]
A genuine, slow-moving threat, strongest in integrity screening, weakest in raw production capacity
AI-native entrants will undercut
codemantra, S4Carlisle and TNQ all ship AI platforms; open source models lower the cost of building [58, 59, 63]
I found no AI-native vendor at scale in the evidence; the entrants named are established vendors; publishers move slowly on validated tools [53]
Open question; this is the risk I can least rule out
The margin proves the thesis wrong

H1 FY27 margin 34.3%; Research margin 48.2%, about 37% to 42% to 45.1% to 48.2% across Q1 FY26 to Q2 FY27; in Q2 FY27 Research EBITDA rose 25.26% on reported revenue growth of only 8.56% (21.71% excluding AJE) [2, 25, 17, 68]

RWS held revenue within 4% of the prior year yet adjusted pre-tax profit fell 43%; a rising margin can also reflect cost resets (Corporate Learning had 19% fewer people) and planning-rate currency [67, 2]
Supportive, not proof: margin is a lagging indicator of price, and the test is whether it holds through the next re-bid cycle
web_blocks.takeaway: The bear thesis as phrased is half right. Unit prices are being negotiated down, and MPS does not deny it. The evidence does not show a collapse. Revenue and margins are rising together, which is the signature of a vendor winning share and volume faster than it concedes price. The thesis becomes dangerous only if two things coincide. Volume must stop compounding, and a re-bid must reset unit rates for a top-five customer.

web_blocks.html: My independent judgment comes in probabilities, not price language. Take the strong-form bear thesis first. It says per-unit deflation outruns volume and mix, so consolidated EBITDA margin settles below FY25's 29.0% within three fiscal years. I put the chance it proves right at about 20% [1]. The weak form says AI keeps deflating unit rates, customers capture a meaningful share of every productivity gain, and MPS has to run faster each year to stand still. I put that at about 80%, because management's own pricing remark concedes it. Next, the Research segment margin of 48.2%. I put the chance it holds within three points over the next eight quarters at about 35%. I put the chance it stays above 40% at about 70%. A 6-point gain in a year includes work still ramping to steady state and hiring ahead, which management itself flags [2]. These are my numbers, not company guidance. They would move on the evidence in the trigger box that follows.

web_blocks.company: RWS Holdings plc (language, localisation and content services)
web_blocks.region_era: United Kingdom / global, FY2024 to FY2025 (machine translation then generative AI)
web_blocks.mechanism: RWS is an outsourced content-services vendor embedded with enterprise and life-sciences clients. It is paid per unit of content, such as translation words and linguistic validation. Clients moved to machine translation and expected AI-driven efficiencies. Traditional translation volumes fell and unit prices came under pressure. The vendor's revenue barely moved. The profit pool underneath shrank, because cost base and mix did not flex as fast as price.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: For the year to 30 September 2025, revenue was £690.1m against £718.2m. That is down 4%, or 0.7% on an organic constant-currency basis. Adjusted profit before tax fell to £60.4m from £106.7m, down 43%. The adjusted margin was about 8.8% against about 14.9%, computed from those figures. The group booked an £88.0m non-cash goodwill impairment and a reported loss before tax of £99.7m. Its own text attributes the Language Services trend to 'declines in traditional translation volumes as clients move to machine translation, and pricing pressure'. TrainAI data-services growth offset part of it [67].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: The earliest damage from AI deflation shows up in margin and profit, not revenue. A 4% revenue slip hid a 43% profit fall. MPS's revenue and margin are both rising, which is the opposite pattern. But this is the template for what failure looks like. Segment margin, especially Research, is the metric to watch each quarter, not the top line. The comparison is imperfect. RWS also absorbed a large integration. MPS sells platform and subscription revenue that RWS's translation core lacked.

web_blocks.company: Wolters Kluwer Health (UpToDate and drug data)
web_blocks.region_era: Netherlands / United States, 2024 to 2025 (generative AI arrives in clinical reference)
web_blocks.mechanism: UpToDate is physician-authored clinical content embedded in hospital workflows and renewed annually by institutions. Its owner was not displaced by general-purpose chatbots. It migrated its largest US institutional customers to an Enterprise platform. It then layered an AI conversational interface (UpToDate Expert AI) on top of validated content. It also integrated with ambient clinical-note vendors. The workflow embed and the trusted content were the moat. AI became an upsell, not a substitute.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: In 2025 the Health division reported revenue of EUR 1,596m and organic growth of 5%. Adjusted operating margin was 32.1% against 30.3% in 2024. Clinical Solutions (57% of divisional revenue) delivered 7% organic growth in both 2025 and 2024, 'driven by good renewal rates for UpToDate'. By the end of 2025 most of the largest US institutional customers had migrated to UpToDate Enterprise. Expert AI launched commercially in October 2025 [65].
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: This is the best-case template for Unbound Medicine. Sticky institutional subscriptions plus validated content give pricing power through a technology shift. The scale mismatch is huge. Unbound is about $9 million of revenue per the Q1 FY27 call, against a EUR 1.6 billion division. The twin proves the mechanism, not MPS's ability to replicate it [25]. It also shows the tell to track: renewal rates, and the ability to keep raising price at renewal.

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: What each twin teaches about where to look
paragraphs: RWS and Wolters Kluwer Health lived through the same technology shift and landed in opposite places. The difference is not that one used AI and the other did not. Both did. The difference is what the customer would have to rebuild. A model can regenerate a translation vendor's output tomorrow. It cannot regenerate a clinician's reference embedded in the hospital workflow. MPS has some of each. The whole question about the business is the mix.

Look at the one number that tells the two stories apart. Management says MPS now earns 45% of revenue from recurring themes and 25% from outcome-based partnerships [25]. If the recurring share keeps rising, MPS is moving toward the Wolters Kluwer side of the ledger. If it stalls, the RWS story is the one to study.

web_blocks.html: What would raise our estimate of business quality: (1) two or more further top-ten publishers awarding multi-year integrity or peer-review mandates alongside production work. (2) Unbound renewal rates at or above the 97% reported at acquisition, while annual price rises keep sticking. (3) The recurring-revenue share management quotes rising from 45% without the Research margin falling. What would lower it: (1) a top-five customer re-bidding production at materially lower unit rates without a matching volume commitment. (2) Research segment margin falling back toward 40% for two consecutive quarters while revenue growth slows to mid-single digits. (3) A large publisher publicly moving integrity screening or composition fully in-house. These are business-quality tests, not price triggers [2, 41].

Finally, the External Learning Hub. I would rather you form your own view than take mine. Everything in the hub was opened and confirmed to load as of 13 November 2026. I have said what each link is worth your time for. MPS's own pages are product marketing. Read them for what the company says it sells, then cross-check against the competitor and industry sources beside them. Two MPS business sites returned a bot-check page to automated retrieval: MPS Interactive and Liberate Global. I dropped them rather than cite what I could not read [69].

web_blocks.title: NARRATOR'S NOTE: How to use the Learning Hub against management's story
paragraphs: A good way to study this company is to hold two documents side by side. One is what management says on the call. The other is what an outsider says about the same thing. Management says 'AI follows businesses that sell hours. We sell outcomes.' [2] The Scholarly Kitchen says production vendors are automating and publishers are exploring in-house tools [43]. Both can be true at once. Your job is to find the evidence that tells you which MPS revenue line belongs to which statement.

The most valuable disclosure that does not yet exist is the revenue split between per-unit production and outcome-based or recurring work. Management gave the 25% and 45% figures on the Q1 FY27 call. It has not published the underlying definitions [25]. When you read the next annual report, look for that split first.

book_paragraphs: Let me ask you something before we talk about moats. If I handed you a manuscript tonight and asked you what the industry around it looks like, would you picture a publisher? Most people do. But the publisher is only the name on the cover. Behind it sits a long chain of people and machines that nobody outside the trade ever sees: the editor who triages the submission, the peer reviewers who are asked to read it for free, the copyeditor, the person who tags it into a structured file, the platform that hosts it, and the librarian who finally pays for it. MPS lives inside that chain. It rarely owns the product, and almost never gets paid by the reader. It gets paid by the publisher, per page, per article, per manuscript reviewed, or lately per year of a subscription.

That payment structure is the first thing I want you to hold on to, because it makes this industry a bargaining game. A handful of enormous publishers, Springer Nature, Elsevier, Wiley, Taylor & Francis and the big university presses, sit on one side of the table. A crowd of vendors, some very old and some very new, sit on the other. The buyer knows precisely what a copyedited page costs everywhere in the world, and when a better tool arrives, the buyer asks to share in the saving. You do not need me to tell you this is uncomfortable for a vendor. What I want to show you is that the discomfort is not new. The Q2 FY27 call put it bluntly. The CEO said: 'With pricing as well, you know, Customers expect to share in our productivity, and they do, but we kind of make that up through more volume, and that’s where the margin kind of comes from.' Read that sentence twice. It admits the pressure, and it claims the escape route.

Is the escape route real? Look at the pool of volume. Article output has been growing at five to six percent a year for a decade, according to the STM trade body and to the Scholarly Kitchen. Submissions are worse: Springer Nature reports submissions up more than thirty percent to 3.1 million in 2025, and one journal told its community that submissions are up forty-two percent since ChatGPT arrived. At the same time, the market's dollar value only grows at a mid-single-digit pace; Delta Think puts the journals market at just under ten billion dollars in 2025 and expects about 5.7% a year to 2028. So units are growing faster than dollars. That is the vendor's opportunity and the vendor's trap in one picture: more things to handle, each paid a little less.

Now meet the people MPS fights with. Straive, formerly SPi Global, is the giant: more than 19,500 people in ten countries, owned by EQT, and now describing itself as a data and AI company rather than a typesetter. Datamatics owns Lumina and TNQTech, and Datamatics itself did nearly two thousand crore rupees of revenue in FY26. Integra, S4Carlisle, KnowledgeWorks Global and Aptara sell more or less the same menu. A newer breed, codemantra for instance, sells AI-first accessibility software. Beside them sit the author-services brands, Editage and Enago, who talk about reaching half a million and two million researchers. And in the clinical world, the incumbents are UpToDate from Wolters Kluwer and Elsevier's ClinicalKey. If you walk through that list, you will notice something quietly important: every one of them says 'AI'. So when MPS says 'AI-first', it is not saying anything that separates it from the field. What separates it, if anything, is what it owns.

What does MPS own? Here is where I want you to slow down, because this is the heart of the moat question. It owns a production engine, DigiCore, that has been refined since 2012. It owns a hosting platform in HighWire, a Stanford-born platform now powered by MPS. It owns the peer-review capacity it got through AJE, and it owns an institutional subscription asset, Unbound Medicine, with ninety-seven percent retention reported at acquisition. Layered on top is a customer approach called star accounts, where a handful of the largest clients get a dedicated executive sponsor and an account director. Management says the average star account now uses five and a half MPS business units, up from two and a half. That number is the closest thing to a moat I can show you in black and white, because a client using five units of one vendor has threaded that vendor through its own workflow.

But I promised you the other side, and I should keep that promise. Think about how a moat is attacked. First, a customer decides to do the work itself; Springer Nature bought a small AI company to build its own integrity screening, and the Scholarly Kitchen reports publishers are weighing in-house options across the whole production chain. Second, a re-bid arrives and everyone's rate card is reset. Third, the technology that was supposed to be a wall becomes a door: a June 2026 Scholarly Kitchen panel, with a Silverchair executive speaking, argued that AI agents will make it far less costly to migrate between platforms, which weakens exactly the switching cost MPS says protects HighWire and DigiCore Pro. And fourth, concentration. In FY26, three customers each exceeded ten percent of the standalone company's revenue. That is not unusual in outsourced publishing, but it means one decision can move a quarter.

So let me test the bear case directly, as you and I would test a witness. The bear says generative AI collapses the price of content production and MPS is a legacy typesetter. Look at what happened to revenue and margin. In the first half of FY27, revenue grew 17.8% and EBITDA grew 39%. The Research segment's margin has climbed from roughly 37% a year or so ago to 42%, then 45.1%, then 48.2% in the latest quarter. If the collapse were happening, we would see the opposite. But I want you to see why I will not stop there. A rising margin can also hide a problem: cost resets, new work still ramping, and a currency planning rate that can flatter profit. And the RWS story, which I will show you in a moment, is a reminder that a vendor's revenue can slip only four percent while its profit falls by two-fifths. Margin is a lagging witness. It tells you what has happened to price, not what will happen at the next re-bid.

So here is my judgment, said the way I would say it across a desk. I think the strong version of the bear thesis, a structural collapse that takes consolidated margins below last year's twenty-nine percent within three years, has roughly a one-in-five chance of being right. I think the weaker version, that AI keeps deflating unit rates and MPS has to run faster each year to stand still, is closer to four-in-five likely, because management has already conceded it. And I think the probability that the Research margin stays within three points of today's 48% over the next two years is closer to one in three. In other words, the business looks sturdier than its sceptics say and more exposed than its management says. That is a sentence worth remembering, because it is the thread through the remaining chapters.

Before you read on, I want to ask you to do something. Open the External Learning Hub and read the two sources I would put first: the Scholarly Kitchen piece on platforms coming apart, and the Unbound acquisition call. Read the bear case and the bull case in one sitting. Then ask yourself the question I will keep asking you: if this vendor walked out tomorrow, what would the customer have to rebuild? Where the honest answer is 'a lot', you have a moat. Where it is 'a model could regenerate it by Tuesday', you have a service with an expiry date.

book_callouts.quote: Relationships and subscriptions are fences; certifications and 'AI-first' are only the gate.

Middle (3 of 5): platform switching costs, delivery cost position, MPS Labs IP, peer-review capacity, scale among fragmented peers.

book_callouts.quote: Same technology shift; opposite outcomes; the difference was what the customer would have to rebuild.

Research margin staying above 40% over eight quarters: about 70%.
Research margin staying within three points of 48.2%: about 35%.

book_subsections.title: The Chain Behind the Cover: Who Pays Whom
paragraphs: Picture a journal article as a parcel moving along a conveyor belt. At the start, a researcher writes it, sometimes with help from an author-services firm that fixes the English and checks the figures. The parcel is submitted, and a journal editorial office, often outsourced, logs it, checks it for plagiarism and fakery, and sends it to reviewers. Each of those steps has a price per parcel. Next comes production: copyediting, composition into a layout, conversion into structured XML, accessibility tagging so that a blind reader's software can follow the figures. Then the parcel is hosted on a platform, indexed, and finally licensed to libraries, or, increasingly, paid for up front by the author's funder as an open-access fee.

Now notice who pays each of those fees. It is the publisher, the society or the author; never the reader. That is why the open-access shift matters to vendors in a way it does not matter to readers. Delta Think says fifty-two percent of articles are now open access but only about a third of the market's value, which means each article brings in less, yet there are more of them. For a vendor paid per parcel, volume is the friend and price is the enemy, and the negotiation never ends.

And here is a piece of the chain that did not exist five years ago: the integrity checkpoint. When paper mills began flooding journals with fabricated submissions and Wiley had to retract well over a thousand Hindawi papers, publishers realised that peer review was a bottleneck and an attack surface at once. They built a shared defence, the STM Integrity Hub, and many began buying screening work. That is a new line of paid work for a vendor with peer-review capacity, and it is the reason management leans so hard on the word 'trust' in its call scripts.

book_subsections.title: Reading the Competitor Table Like a Buyer
paragraphs: Put yourself in a publisher's procurement chair. You have a list of vendors, and you are about to decide who gets your next three-to-five-year contract. You ask what you would ask in any category: who is big enough to survive, who has the security certificates my auditors need, who has the lowest cost per page, who will answer the phone at midnight, and who can show me that the AI really works. For most of those questions, the vendors are indistinguishable on paper. Every one has ISO certificates; every one will say 'AI-powered'. The decision turns on a quieter question: who is already woven into my workflow, so that switching is a project rather than a purchase order?

That is why MPS's cross-sell index matters more than its AI slogans. A publisher that uses MPS for production, peer review, hosting and accessibility has four reasons to stay, and each reason is attached to a different internal team at the publisher. A re-bid has to persuade all four. By contrast, a vendor that only does composition for that publisher faces a single procurement manager and a single price comparison. This is why large buyers consolidating their vendor lists tends to favour the broad, integrated supplier, and it is the strongest argument management has made that vendor consolidation benefits scale players.

But do not forget the other side of the table. A large publisher that has seen its vendors deliver ever-greater productivity is not going to pay last year's rates for this year's work. Management knows this; the CEO has said customers expect to share in the productivity. So the real contest is whether MPS can add enough new lines of work to each client to replace the rate it gives back, and whether those new lines, integrity, peer review, platforms, are protected from the next wave of in-house tools. That is the quiet game you are watching.

book_subsections.title: Two Strangers Who Teach Us: RWS and Wolters Kluwer Health
paragraphs: I want to introduce you to two companies that have nothing to do with MPS and everything to teach us. The first is RWS, a British translation and content-services firm with clients in life sciences and technology. When machine translation, and then generative AI, arrived, RWS's clients began sending fewer words to human translators and asking for AI-driven efficiencies on the rest. In the year to September 2025, RWS's revenue slipped only four percent. Yet its adjusted profit before tax fell by forty-three percent, and it wrote off eighty-eight million pounds of goodwill. Do you see the pattern? The revenue number was a bystander; the profit number took the hit. That is the first thing I want you to look for in any outsourced content business.

The second is Wolters Kluwer Health, home of UpToDate, a clinical reference that doctors consult in the middle of a ward round. Faced with the same generative AI wave, it did not retreat. It migrated its biggest US hospital customers to an enterprise platform and added an AI conversational layer built on its physician-authored content. In 2025, Health grew organically by five percent and its margin rose from 30.3 to 32.1%, with clinical solutions growing seven percent for two years running, driven by renewals. The difference between the two stories is not talent or technology. It is what the customer would have to rebuild: a model can regenerate a translated paragraph, but it cannot regenerate a hospital's embedded clinical workflow overnight.

Where does MPS sit between those two poles? Partly on each. The production and accessibility work looks closer to RWS. Unbound Medicine looks like a tiny cousin of UpToDate, with ninety-seven percent retention and annual price rises, but it is only nine million dollars of revenue, so the comparison proves the mechanism, not the scale. The CEO's own line on the Q2 FY27 call was: 'AI follows businesses that sell hours. We sell outcomes.' Whether that is a description or an aspiration depends on how fast the recurring and outcome-based share rises. Management says 45% of revenue is recurring and 25% is outcome-based today. If those shares keep climbing, you are watching a vendor migrate from the RWS side of the ledger toward the Wolters Kluwer side. If they stall, you will have your answer to the bear case sooner than you expect.
